ASM Khalequzzaman, Advocate—For the Petitioner 
A Baset Majumder, Senior Advocate—For the Respondent No. 3
M Khaled Ahmed, Advocate—For the Respondent No. 2
parties:
Mazakat Harun. ------Petitioner
vs
Artha Rin Adalat No. 1, Dhaka and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md. Badruzzaman J : On an application under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh this Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned Order No. 90 dated 19-3-2012 (Annexure-A) passed by the Artha Rin Adalat No. 1, Dhaka, in Artha Rin Execution Case No. 79 of 1998 arising out of Artha Rin Suit No. 192 of 1995 setting-aside the auction proceeding and cancelling the sale certificate dated 19-11-2005 issued in favour of the petitioner regarding mortgage property, now pending in the Court of Artha Rin Adalat No. 1, Dhaka should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

 2. The background leading to the issuance of the Rule, in short, is that the Respondent No. 2. Bangladesh Krishi Bank Limited being financial institution (herein after referred to as the respondent Bank) filed Artha Rin Suit No. 192 of 1995 before the Artha Rin Adalat for recovery of outstanding dues to the tune of Taka 1,22,50,673 as on 29-11-1995 and the said suit was decreed on 14-11-1996 exparte. The judgment-debtor being failed to pay the decretal dues the respondent Bank filed Artha Execution Case No. 79 of 1998 for recovery of the decretal dues. The decree-holder being failed to sell the mortgage property by publishing notice under section 33(4) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 (hereinafter referred to as the Ain 2003) again published a notice under section 33(4) of the Ain on 1-10-2005 for selling the mortgaged property in auction fixing 23-10-2005 for auction sale. 

 3. The petitioner participated in the auction and became the highest bidder and his bid was accepted by the Artha Rin Adalat (herein after referred to as the Adalat) on 23-10-2005 and the sale was confirmed on 24-11-2005 and sale certificate was issued and registered on 30-11-2005. While the delivery of possession of the mortgage property was under process the judgment-debtor, with ulterior motive filed Writ Petition No. 903 of 2006 and thereafter Writ Petition No. 7364 of 2009 and Writ Petition No. 1926 of 2011 before the High Court Division and obtained Rule and order of stay of all further proceeding of the execution case and, as such, the possession of the property could not be delivered to the auction purchaser petitioner. Ultimately after disposal of the aforesaid writ petitions the auction purchaser filed an application for delivery of possession of the property sold in auction but it could not be delivered in favour of the auction purchaser as the judgment-debtor resisted to give delivery of possession and, as such, the auction purchaser filed an application for delivery of possession with the help of police force and by order of the Adalat deposited Taka 60,940.40 for the expense of the police force. At this stage the judgment-debtor on 27-7-2011 filed Miscellaneous Case No. 19 of 2011 under Order XXI, rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure (herein after referred to as the Code) for setting-aside the auction which was withdrawn on 1-1-2012 and on the same date the judgment-debtor filed an application without mentioning any provision of law praying for settlement to resolve the dispute and also for setting-aside sale certificate issued in favour of the auction purchaser. The auction purchaser filed written objection against the said application. 

 6. Mr. ASM Khalequzzaman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner submits that the learned Judge of the Adalat travelled beyond its jurisdiction in setting-aside the sale certificate after confirmation of sale and registration thereof with the concerned Sub-Registry Office on 30-11-2005. Mr. Zaman further submits that the respondent No. 3, being judgment-debtor, had the opportunity to have the said sale set-aside under Order XXI, rule 89 or 90 of the Code within 30 days from the date of sale but having not so done, the judgment debtor actually waived his right in setting-aside the auction sale. The learned Advocate further submits that admittedly the auction sale of the property in question has been confirmed vide order dated 24-11-2005, consequently the sale became absolute conferring good title to the auction purchaser petitioner related back to the date of sale in view of the provisions of section 65 of the Code. Accordingly, depositing the decretal amount after confirmation of sale will not go to create any legal right in favour of the judgment-debtor to receive back the schedule property. The learned Advocate again submits that under section 57 of the Ain empowers the Adalat to pass “পরিপূরক” order to prevent abuse of the process of the Adalat. He also submits that though section 38 provides settlement of dispute at any stage of execution proceeding but considering the facts and circumstances of the case if such prayer of the judgment-debtor is entertained at this stage it will tantamount to declare title of the auction purchaser, nugatory. The learned Advocate further submits that once an auction process is completed no relief is available against such auction sale but the mortgagor may proceed against the mortgagee Bank for compensation, if it is proved that there was illegality in the auction process. He lastly submits that the judgment-debtor, after confirmation of auction sale, dragged the matter for more than 6 (six) years by filing Writ Petition Nos. 903 of 2006, 7364 of 2009 and 1926 of 2011 one after another and in all the writ petitions Rule was discharged and thereafter the judgment-debtor filed another application under order XXI, rule 90 of the Code on 27-7-2011 for setting-aside the auction sale which was with-drawn by him on 1-1-2012 and as a last resort for dragging the matter, filed the application for settlement of the dispute and for setting-aside auction sale with frivolous grounds, which was allowed by the Adalat without any sanction of law by the impugned order and, as such, the same should be declared to have been passed without jurisdiction and of no legal effect. In support his contention the learned Advocate has relied upon a decision of the case of Sonali Bank vs Artha Rin Adalat, Narayanganj, reported in 15 MLR (AD) 20 = 62 DLR (AD) 231. 

 7. Mr. Abdul Basel Majumder, the learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of respondent No. 3 mainly supports the order passed by the Adalat and submits that as the auction purchaser has got no possession of the property sold in auction yet it cannot be said that the execution proceeding has been ended with the confirmation of auction sale and the door of the judgment-debtor has shut forever to settle the dispute upon paying the decretal amount with the Bank within the preview of section 38 of the Ain. The learned Advocate further submits that the Adalat has jurisdiction under section 57 of the AM to pass any appropriate order for securing ends of justice. The learned Advocate by referring an unreported judgment of the Appellate Division passed in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 2272 of 2009 of the case of Golam Azam Choudhury vs Md. Azizur Rahman submits that the Appellate Division has consistently taken equitable approach when the judgment debtor came forward to pay the entire decretal dues by allowing the judgment-debtor to retain his property sold in auction subject to payment of decretal amount as well as solatium at the rate of 10% to the auction purchaser. The learned Advocate finally submits that considering the facts and circumstances of the case neither the decree-holder Bank nor the auction purchaser shall suffer any loss if the respondent No. 3 is allowed to pay the decretal dues with a compensation at the rate of 10% to the auction purchaser as the property sold in auction has not handed over to the auction purchaser through the process of the Court yet. 

 14. There is no provision in the Code of Civil Procedure of 1908 either under Order XXI or elsewhere which provides that the sale is not to be confirmed or to be set-aside if it be found that the decree under which the sale was ordered has been reversed before the confirmation of sale. It does not seem ever to have been doubted that once the sale is confirmed the judgment-debtor is not entitled to get back the property even if he succeeds thereafter in having the decree against him reversed. This view finds support in the case of Janak Raj vs Gurdial Singh, reported in AIR (1967) (SC) 608. 

 15. In the case of 15 MLR (AD) 20 as cited by the learned Advocate for the petitioner our apex Court held:— 

 "It appears that the leave petitioner bank is negligent in not informing the executing Court about the fact of restoration of the rule and stay dated 15-6-2006 and that the leave petitioner bank by filing an application on 25-6-2006 prayed for receiving the pay order submitted by the auction purchaser in Court and it appears from the impugned judgment and order passed, by the High Court Division that the leave petitioner bank has already encashed the pay order and thereby accepted the auction sale. In view of the provision of law  to the effect that once the auction sale is  complete no relief is available against such  auction sale but the mortgagor may proceed against the mortgagee bank for  any compensation. if it is proved that there  was illegality in the auction sale. In the instant case, it is not such case rather if appears that at the instance of the decree holder bank auction was held and ultimately the decree holder bank has withdrawn the money deposited by the auction purchasers. After the auction process is completed, proceeding with the execution case is redundant. " 

 18. Now, the judgment-debtor taking the advantage of the clause “ ডিক্রী ধারাবাহিকতায় জারী কা্র্যক্রম থাকার যে কোন পর্যায়ে” is coming forward with an offer to settle the dispute with the decree holder bank upon paying the decretal amount. Considering the same if the claim of the judgment debtor is entertained at this stage it will tantamount to declare the title, which has been lawfully vested upon the auction purchaser in view of Order XXI, rule 92 read with section 65 of the Code, nugatory. A Division Bench, of this Division in an unreported decision in the case of Mrs. Rokeya Afroja vs Judge, Artha Rin Adalat No. 4 (Writ Petition No. 8549 of 2005) in the similar situation made the following observation:— 

 22. In view of the above observation, let us now examine the facts and circumstances of the instant case. It appears from the record that the mortgage property was sold in auction on 23-10-2005 and the petitioner became the highest bidder and his bid was excepted by the Adalat on 23-11-2005 and sale was confirmed as per rule 92 of Order XXI of the Code on 24-11-2005 and accordingly the sale certificate was issued in favour of the auction purchaser as per rule 94 which was registered before the concerned Sub-register on 13-11-2005. It is also admitted that the judgment-debtor after laps of long time filed Miscellaneous Case No. 19 of 2011 on 27-7-2011 under Order XXI, rule 90 of the Code for setting-aside the auction sale which was withdrawn on 1-1-2012 and on the same date the judgment-debtor filed an application for settlement of the dispute with the decree holder and for setting-aside the sale certificate and the Adalat after hearing both the parties on 19-3-2012 passed the following order:— 

 23. It has already been observed above that confirmation of sale confers absolute title to the purchaser, be he a stranger or a decree holder. The same view has been mandated in the case of Abdul vs Ramanna reported in AIR 1945 (Madras)161 and with that the executing Court becomes functous officio, as has been found in the case of Bijoy Krishna Paik and another vs Montajuddin Sheikh reported in 12 DLR, 631 and after auction sale is complete no relief is available against such auction sale as observed in, 15 MLR (AD) 608. Accordingly the issue of delivery of possession in favour of the auction purchaser is merely matters of procedural acts of the Adalat involving no issue for judicial adjudication as has already been observed in the case of Sagar Mahila Vidyalaya, Sagar vs Pandit Sadasiv Rao Harshe 1991 3 SCC (SC) 588. As such the contention of Mr. Majumder that without giving delivery of possession of the property sold in auction to the auction purchaser, execution case cannot come to an end with the confirmation of sale has no leg to stand in the eye of judicial pronouncements as discussed above. 

 24. Hence, it can clearly be found that once sale has become confirmed and made absolute under Order XXI, rule 92 of the Code the judgment debtor is debarred by the statute from seeking any shelter of law by depositing the decretal amount before the Court and thereby in effect to have the sale set-aside as because the rights so have been accrued upon the auction purchaser by operation of law cannot be taken away by the judgment debtor in the manner as has been posed by the judgment-debtor in the present case except upon setting-aside the sale on the ground of practicing fraud or material irregularity in publishing or conducting the sale under Order XXI, rule 90 of the Code. The decision as referred to by Mr. Majumder passed in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 2272 of 2009 has also no manner of application considering the facts and circumstances of the present case.
